text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The Left Party will leave party negotiations about what sources of energy Sweden should rely on in the future if Energy Minister Anders Sundstrom insists on closing the first nuclear power reactor as late as in 2001, according to the party's energy negotiator Lennart Beijer.

- The Swedish shareholders' association Aktiespararna's actions during the bidding for mortgage bank Stadshypotek could undermine its credibility as impartial representative for small shareholders. The association recommended insurer Skandia and Stadshypotek's proposal to merge even when several market players started questioning the benefits of the merger.

- A law is needed against health care companies after a profit, according to the national association for disabled. The call for such a law follows complaints about a health care company that posted a profit of six million crowns last year while being criticised for mistreating patients.

- The government's strong focus on wage negotiations has caused unions and employers to search for new solutions and currently, the situation is better than ever for creating a system that will lead to long-term wage increases in line with other European countries' wage growth. Previously, Sweden has often had much larger wage rises than other European countries.

- Although industrial positions, such as engineers and technicians, constitute the work opportunities of the future, young people are not interested, a new report from industrial association Industriforbundet shows.

- Shares that have fallen this year are likely to see large sell-outs around the year-end as investors swap losses against gains for tax reasons. Among dangerous shares are truck maker Scania and non-invasive surgery products group Elekta.

- The Swedish labour market board is not doing a good job of directing billions of crowns in subsidies from the European Union to Swedish companies, according to a report from the National Audit Office.

- The Liberal Party is on its way back into party negotiations about what sources of energy Sweden should rely on in the future, according to newspaper sources. The liberals and the conservatives were previously shut out of negotiations as they are against phasing out Swedish nuclear power before reactors become too old to function safely.
